analysis.one_liner: Extends minimum wage and overtime to agency-employed home care aides and funds workforce tracking and training grants.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 8 cosponsors including the committee chairman, was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a markup or a vote before the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would close a loophole in federal wage law that lets home care agencies pay aides without minimum wage or overtime protections, keeping the exemption only for truly casual arrangements like a family hiring a sitter a few hours a week. It would also require states to report annually on whether they have enough direct care workers to meet long-term care needs, and would fund grants to recruit, train, and retain these workers. It never got a committee vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Direct care workers — home health aides, personal care aides, and nursing assistants who care for elderly and disabled people. The bill's findings note that 45 percent of these workers live at or below the poverty level, average annual income is about $17,000, and more than 1 in 4 lack health insurance. Agency-employed aides would gain minimum wage and overtime rights for the first time. The roughly 10 million Americans who need long-term care would also benefit from a more stable, better-trained workforce.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-paid home care aides and care recipients

how_it_helps.text: Amends the Fair Labor Standards Act so the 'companionship services' exemption from minimum wage and overtime applies only to casual, intermittent work — not to workers whose vocation is caregiving or who are employed by an agency rather than a family [S2][S3].

Keeps the exemption for genuine casual arrangements: a household employer is exempt only if the aide works five hours a week or less and no more than twelve weeks a year, so family flexibility is preserved while agency-employed workers gain protections [S3].

Requires every state Medicaid program to file an annual report detailing its direct care workforce — headcounts, turnover, vacancies, average wages, and benefits — so shortages are documented instead of invisible [S2][S3].

Creates a federal monitoring program for the direct care workforce and authorizes grants to states and tribes to build data systems, plus competitive three-year grants specifically to improve recruitment, retention, and training — including initiatives to raise wages and benefits and build career ladders [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Home care and home health agencies, which would lose the wage-and-overtime exemption they have operated under since 1974 and would owe minimum wage and overtime to their aides; those costs would flow through to families who hire agencies and to state Medicaid budgets. The grant programs would be paid for with federal appropriations, and states would take on new annual reporting duties.
analysis.who_pays_short: Home care agencies and Medicaid budgets

drawbacks.text: Ending the overtime and minimum wage exemption raises labor costs for home care agencies; those costs would likely be passed on to families paying privately and to state Medicaid programs that fund home-based care [S3].

The grant programs are authorized at 'such sums as may be necessary' — meaning they would still need Congress to actually appropriate the money each year, so the training and wage-improvement grants were not guaranteed funding [S3].
The bill adds a new annual reporting mandate for every state Medicaid agency, an administrative burden for state governments [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The wage protections address a real and documented problem — workers earning around $17,000 a year, nearly half living in or near poverty — and the bill was deliberately drawn to leave casual family arrangements (under five hours a week) exempt, limiting the disruption. The main honest cost is the pass-through of wage expenses to families and Medicaid. The data-collection and grant portions are low-cost but also lower-impact, and the grants depended on future appropriations.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate health committee the day it was introduced and never received a markup, a vote, or floor time before the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Senator Robert Casey Jr. of Pennsylvania introduced the bill on June 23, 2011, joined as original cosponsors by Senators Tom Harkin and Bernie Sanders; it was read twice and referred the same day to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S1][S3][S5].
Eight senators cosponsored the bill — seven Democrats and one Independent. No Republican cosponsored it [S4].
The action history shows no further action after the committee referral: no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote for the rest of the Congress [S5].
The Congress ended on January 3, 2013, and the bill died with it; the committee that received the referral was chaired by one of the bill's own original cosponsors [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Home care agencies kept the exemption that allows them to pay aides without minimum wage or overtime, avoiding the new labor costs the bill would have imposed. The low-paid direct care workforce, whose poverty and wage figures the bill itself documented, gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Home care agencies; the workers gained nothing

industries.industry: Home care and home health agencies
industries.note: The bill would strip these agencies of the federal wage-and-overtime exemption their industry has operated under since 1974, requiring minimum wage and overtime for agency-employed aides. The exemption keeps aide pay low, which is exactly the poverty-level compensation the bill documents; the industry's savings come at the workers' expense.

The bill imposes no new wage rules beyond home care agencies, but the annual state reporting on workforce adequacy would document staffing shortages and turnover in nursing homes and other long-term care settings, creating public pressure the industry has not had.
